text: Hey, everybody, let's talk about the Hebrew word  elohim, and specifically how this grammatically
plural noun can be used in reference to individual  deities. And there are three explanations I
want to talk about today. Two that don't really  work and one that is probably the one we should
prefer. Now, the first is the earliest the most  traditional: the idea of the "plural of majesty."
And the idea here is that by using the plural  of this noun, you're not just referring to
any run-of-the-mill example of this noun, but  you are intensifying, you are multiplying the
grandeur, the majesty of this noun. So this  is this uh awesome example of this noun.
Now, this doesn't work for a handful  of reasons. Probably the two biggest   are that this word is used to refer to foreign  deities all the time, and so you're not really
amplifying these deities as these particularly  awesome examples of deity. Additionally,
this construction is not unique to the word for  god. We see it with other words in the Hebrew
Bible and we see it in other words in other  languages, related semitic languages, and most
of the time there's no way it's being used to  amplify the majesty of anything. For instance,
there's a word—there's a language where the word  for slave can be used in the plural to refer
to an individual slave. And so scholars said,  "Well, maybe this is the plural of humility,"
but that just uses the opposite concept to account  for the exact same feature of the language. So
that does not work. Now, in the 19th century, the  famous Hebrew grammarian Wilhelm Gesenius came up
with another way to explain the plural of majesty,  and he said there were two things going on.
One was that this was a variety of the abstract  plural. In Hebrew you can take a singular noun
and you can use the plural to refer not to  numerical plurals but to an abstraction of the
noun. So the Hebrew word אב, father: when you put  it in the plural—and it has an unusual plural but
that doesn't matter right now—אבות can  mean "fathers" or it can mean "fatherhood,"
the abstract quality of being a father. And  the other thing he said that was going on was
an intensive plural. So similar to the plural  of majesty, but instead of just talking about
majesty, what you are amplifying or intensifying  is whatever is prototypical of that noun.
So it would be a plural of majesty with  reference to God because that's considered
prototypical of deity. Now, there are problems  with this as well. To begin, majesty, power,
glory are not necessarily prototypical of all  deity. In the Hebrew Bible it's prototypical of
the rhetoric of praise directed at YHWH,  the God of Israel, but not at all deities,
and this raises another problem: singular elohim  is used in reference to foreign deities, including
in polemical speech. Why would you be emphasizing  the majesty, the power, the glory of other deities
while you are saying they are worthless and  less than nothing? That doesn't make much sense.
And a final reason this does not  make much sense is because there   are no indications anywhere in the biblical text  that there is any semantic difference whatsoever
between singular elohim and just el or eloah. In  fact, these words get interchanged in parallel and
quoted passages, and so there does not seem to be  anything special about the sense of the singular
use of elohim. It just seems to mean "god." Now,  one of the things that Gesenius did was provide
a little hint of a better explanation for what  might be going on here. Toward the end of his
explanation, he says, "Hence אלהים may have been  used originally not only as a numerical but also
as an abstract plural (corresponding  to the Latin numen, and our Godhead),
and, like other abstracts of the same kind,  have been transferred to a concrete single god
(even of the heathen)." So this idea that  it was an abstract plural that then became
used as a reference to an individual deity,  even foreign deities, makes up for the gap
in this plural of majesty explanation. But he  didn't really expound on that. It didn't get
expounded on until the 2001 book, A Reassessment  of Biblical Elohim, by Joel Burnett, where Joel
tracks down this construction in Hebrew and in  related languages, and argues that that is the
best explanation—that it is a concretized abstract  plural. In other words, very early on—even before
the individuation of Hebrew as a language—this  plural elohim was used in the abstract to refer
to the abstract qualities of deity—to divinity—but  then was used so frequently in reference to
specific deities that it became  concretized—a concretized abstract plural.
And there are two things that this theory  accounts for that I think are interesting.
One if we go to the abstraction, so we take  "god" and then we go to the abstraction,   "divinity," and then we concretize it as  "deity," that's not marked for gender,
coming from an abstraction, and this is why the  singular elohim can be used to refer to goddesses.
So, for instance, 1 Kings 11:33: the goddess  of the Sidonians is referred to as an elohim,
even though it is a female deity.  Another thing that it can account for
is the adjectival use of elohim. So this is  probably what's going on in what some people call
the superlative use of elohim—that it means  "great" or "most great" or something like
that—it probably is just an adjectival use so  of god—divine—and if we're coming from this
abstraction—divinity back to deity—then that would  allow that word to be used adjectivally, referring
to the divine qualities that a given noun has. And  so I would argue that Burnett's theory, for the
time being at least, makes much better sense than  a plural of majesty—whether the original theory or
Gesenius's theory—this makes much better sense  of it. And so how do we tell in the Hebrew Bible
if our occurrence of elohim is a reference  to an individual deity or a plural deity?
It's not incredibly difficult. There are  only a few debated examples, but you just
look at the verbs and the pronouns, because  the plural use is going to have plural verbs:
"they are doing this," and the singular use  is going to have singular verbs. And so the
very first verse of the Hebrew Bible—בראשית ברא  אלהים—bara is a finite verb in the singular. So
the elohim there is singular. "God created." So  the first verse does not say "the gods created,"
it just says "God created," because the verb  is in the singular. And you also have pronouns   that will be in the singular or the plural.  Now there are some debated examples. You have
plural verbs being used in reference to elohim  being put in the mouth of people who are supposed
to be referring to the God of Israel. So,  for instance, Genesis 20 verse 13, Abraham
tells Abimelech, "when the gods caused me to  wander," but if you look that up in your Bible,
pretty much nobody translates it in the plural,  because they think Abraham is referring to   the God of Israel, so they're saying, "Man,  we're just going to take this as a singular."
And the argument there is that there is kind of a  harmonization going on where the plural noun—the
person speaking or writing is like, "I want to  make that plural just because the noun is plural,"
and while that's plausible, it doesn't really  make much sense because it is so rare. We don't
see this happening a lot, in fact the only times  we ever see it happening [in narrative] are in   places where the authors use plural verbs and  readers don't want to understand it in the plural.
And so this example in Genesis 20:13: Abraham is  probably just using the plural—and whether you
want to say this is Abraham deferring to the  polytheistic sensitivities of Abimelech, uh,
that's—you can say that, but you should probably  still translate it in the plural. Another
explanation is that this is an earlier form of the  story where Abraham is just referring to plural
gods, and there's an argument to make for that as  well. In fact, the Tetragrammaton [YHWH] doesn't   occur throughout Genesis 20 except in the very  last verse, which is most likely an editorial
addition, because it is giving information that  the narrator thinks you already have. So in verse
17—after they have made their peace—verse 17 says,  "So Elohim healed Abimelech, and his wife, and all
the women in his household," and then verse 18  says, "by the way YHWH had closed up the wombs
of all the women in his household." So that's the  only time the Tetragrammaton occurs, and it is
in what is most likely an editorial addition that  is giving you information you should have already
had. So this is probably an earlier narrative that  is being woven into a broader narrative that uses
the Tetragrammaton, the divine name. So I would  say that Abraham is probably—we should interpret
that as Abraham referring to plural gods and uh  just not get too upset about that. So, those are
the three reasons people have come up with for  explaining why this grammatically plural noun
can be used in reference to individual deities.  The concretized abstract plural reading I suggest   makes the most sense of things, uh, and, yeah, I  hope that's given you something to think about.
